claim: Intrinsically disordered transcription factor transactivation domains (TADs) function through structural plasticity, adopting ordered conformations when bound to transcriptional co-regulators.
source: Intrinsically disordered transcription factor transactivation domains (TADs) function through structural plasticity, adopting ordered conformations when bound to transcriptional co-regulators.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, supported by the general understanding of TAD behavior.

claim: Many transcription factors contain a negative regulatory domain (NRD) that suppresses recruitment of transcriptional machinery through autoregulation of the TAD.
source: Many transcription factors contain a negative regulatory domain (NRD) that suppresses recruitment of transcriptional machinery through autoregulation of the TAD.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about transcription factors.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD and TAD are primarily intrinsically disordered domains.
source: We observe that while both the FoxM1 NRD and TAD are primarily intrinsically disordered domains, they associate and adopt a structured conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section with CD and NMR data.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD and TAD associate and adopt a structured conformation.
source: We observe that while both the FoxM1 NRD and TAD are primarily intrinsically disordered domains, they associate and adopt a structured conformation.
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural data and ITC binding measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Plk1 and Cdk kinases cooperate to phosphorylate FoxM1.
source: We identify how Plk1 and Cdk kinases cooperate to phosphorylate FoxM1, which releases the TAD into a disordered conformation that then associates with the TAZ2 or KIX domains of the transcriptional co-activator CBP.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assays, mass spectrometry data, and ITC binding measurements showing Cdk phosphorylation creates Plk1 binding sites.

claim: Phosphorylation by Plk1 and Cdk releases the FoxM1 TAD into a disordered conformation.
source: We identify how Plk1 and Cdk kinases cooperate to phosphorylate FoxM1, which releases the TAD into a disordered conformation that then associates with the TAZ2 or KIX domains of the transcriptional co-activator CBP.
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy and NMR data showing disorder in the phosphorylated state.

claim: The released FoxM1 TAD associates with the TAZ2 or KIX domains of the transcriptional co-activator CBP.
source: We identify how Plk1 and Cdk kinases cooperate to phosphorylate FoxM1, which releases the TAD into a disordered conformation that then associates with the TAZ2 or KIX domains of the transcriptional co-activator CBP.
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding measurements showing TAD binding to TAZ2 and KIX domains.

claim: The FoxM1 TAD undergoes switching between disordered and different ordered structures.
source: Our results support a mechanism of FoxM1 regulation in which the TAD undergoes switching between disordered and different ordered structures.
evidence: This is supported by NMR and CD data showing different structural states of the TAD in different contexts.

claim: TADs consist of structurally disordered domains.
source: TADs consist of structurally disordered domains, which facilitate adaptable association with multiple protein partners and, in some contexts, form interaction network hubs within liquid condensates (Cho et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Structurally disordered TADs facilitate adaptable association with multiple protein partners.
source: TADs consist of structurally disordered domains, which facilitate adaptable association with multiple protein partners and, in some contexts, form interaction network hubs within liquid condensates (Cho et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TADs can form interaction network hubs within liquid condensates.
source: TADs consist of structurally disordered domains, which facilitate adaptable association with multiple protein partners and, in some contexts, form interaction network hubs within liquid condensates (Cho et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TAD accessibility can be modulated through cellular localization, co-factor binding, ligand binding, posttranslational modifications, protein stability, phase separation, or oligomerization.
source: Accessibility can be modulated through cellular localization, co-factor binding, ligand binding, posttranslational modifications, protein stability, phase separation, or oligomerization (Bah et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many transcription factors contain a negative regulatory domain (NRD) that is thought to bind and inhibit the TAD.
source: Many transcription factors, including critical regulators of cell division, contain a negative regulatory domain (NRD) that is thought to bind and inhibit the TAD (Kim et al., 1999; Park et al., 2008b; Ramsay and Gonda, 2008; Shi et al., 1995; Spengler and Brattain, 2006; Wierstra and Alves, 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 is critical for dividing cells.
source: FoxM1 is critical for dividing cells, as it activates expression of genes that facilitate mitotic entry, the mitotic program, and proper cell-cycle progression (Fu et al., 2008; Korver et al., 1997; Korver et al., 1998; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 activates expression of genes that facilitate mitotic entry, the mitotic program, and proper cell-cycle progression.
source: FoxM1 is critical for dividing cells, as it activates expression of genes that facilitate mitotic entry, the mitotic program, and proper cell-cycle progression (Fu et al., 2008; Korver et al., 1997; Korver et al., 1998; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 expression is normally confined to dividing cells.
source: FoxM1 expression is normally confined to dividing cells and is found most commonly in embryogenesis, hematopoiesis, and tissue repair (Korver et al., 1997; Ramakrishna et al., 2007; Ustiyan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 is found most commonly in embryogenesis, hematopoiesis, and tissue repair.
source: FoxM1 expression is normally confined to dividing cells and is found most commonly in embryogenesis, hematopoiesis, and tissue repair (Korver et al., 1997; Ramakrishna et al., 2007; Ustiyan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 is essential for proper development.
source: FoxM1 is essential for proper development; null mice exhibit an embryonic lethal phenotype due to liver, blood, heart, and lung abnormalities resulting from proliferation defects (Ramakrishna et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 null mice exhibit an embryonic lethal phenotype due to liver, blood, heart, and lung abnormalities resulting from proliferation defects.
source: FoxM1 is essential for proper development; null mice exhibit an embryonic lethal phenotype due to liver, blood, heart, and lung abnormalities resulting from proliferation defects (Ramakrishna et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Aberrant expression and misregulation of FoxM1 are associated with multiple cancers.
source: Aberrant expression and misregulation of FoxM1 are associated with multiple cancers and are directly related to increased proliferation, metastasis, chemoresistance, and poor therapeutic prognosis (Koo et al., 2012; Myatt and Lam, 2007; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 aberrant expression is directly related to increased proliferation, metastasis, chemoresistance, and poor therapeutic prognosis.
source: Aberrant expression and misregulation of FoxM1 are associated with multiple cancers and are directly related to increased proliferation, metastasis, chemoresistance, and poor therapeutic prognosis (Koo et al., 2012; Myatt and Lam, 2007; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 misregulation at both the transcriptional and protein level has been observed in adenocarcinomas, breast cancer, squamous cell carcinomas, leukemia, lymphoma, and many additional malignancies.
source: FoxM1 misregulation at both the transcriptional and protein level has been observed in adenocarcinomas, breast cancer, squamous cell carcinomas, leukemia, lymphoma, and many additional malignancies (Kwok et al., 2010; Millour et al., 2010; Park et al., 2011; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011; Xu et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 activates tumor metastasis.
source: Several studies have shown that FoxM1 activates tumor metastasis, mediates drug resistance, and regulates pluripotency-associated genes responsible for maintaining tumor cells in their undifferentiated state (Carr et al., 2010; Kwok et al., 2010; Millour et al., 2010; Park et al., 2011; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Weigelt et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 mediates drug resistance.
source: Several studies have shown that FoxM1 activates tumor metastasis, mediates drug resistance, and regulates pluripotency-associated genes responsible for maintaining tumor cells in their undifferentiated state (Carr et al., 2010; Kwok et al., 2010; Millour et al., 2010; Park et al., 2011; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Weigelt et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 regulates pluripotency-associated genes responsible for maintaining tumor cells in their undifferentiated state.
source: Several studies have shown that FoxM1 activates tumor metastasis, mediates drug resistance, and regulates pluripotency-associated genes responsible for maintaining tumor cells in their undifferentiated state (Carr et al., 2010; Kwok et al., 2010; Millour et al., 2010; Park et al., 2011; Raychaudhuri and Park, 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Weigelt et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of FoxM1 in cancer cells inhibits tumor development and growth.
source: Additionally, deletion of FoxM1 in cancer cells inhibits tumor development and growth and leads to increased apoptosis (Kalinichenko et al., 2004; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of FoxM1 in cancer cells leads to increased apoptosis.
source: Additionally, deletion of FoxM1 in cancer cells inhibits tumor development and growth and leads to increased apoptosis (Kalinichenko et al., 2004; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 contains four distinct functional domains: a negative regulatory domain (NRD), a DNA binding domain (DBD), a region containing several cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) consensus sites (CSR), and a TAD.
source: FoxM1 contains four distinct functional domains (Figure 1A): a negative regulatory domain (NRD), a DNA binding domain (DBD), a region containing several cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) consensus sites (called here the Cdk site region or CSR) and a TAD (Anders et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2008; Littler et al., 2010; Major et al., 2004; Park et al., 2008b; Wierstra and Alves, 2006a; Wierstra and Alves, 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The FoxM1 DBD is the only region with a known well-ordered structure.
source: The DBD is the only region with a known well-ordered structure; it binds to promoter sequences of many cell-cycle regulated genes (Littler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The FoxM1 DBD binds to promoter sequences of many cell-cycle regulated genes.
source: The DBD is the only region with a known well-ordered structure; it binds to promoter sequences of many cell-cycle regulated genes (Littler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD suppresses FoxM1 activity in transcription reporter assays.
source: The NRD suppresses FoxM1 activity in transcription reporter assays, and it has been proposed that the NRD binds and sequesters the TAD from its association with the co-activators CBP and p300 (Laoukili et al., 2008a; Major et al., 2004; Park et al., 2008b; Wierstra and Alves, 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It has been proposed that the FoxM1 NRD binds and sequesters the TAD from its association with the co-activators CBP and p300.
source: The NRD suppresses FoxM1 activity in transcription reporter assays, and it has been proposed that the NRD binds and sequesters the TAD from its association with the co-activators CBP and p300 (Laoukili et al., 2008a; Major et al., 2004; Park et al., 2008b; Wierstra and Alves, 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation by either Cdks or polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1) inhibits repressive activity of the FoxM1 NRD in transcription reporter assays.
source: Phosphorylation by either Cdks or polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1) inhibits repressive activity of the NRD in these assays (Anders et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2008; Laoukili et al., 2008a; Major et al., 2004; Park et al., 2008b), but it is not clear how this activation step occurs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD (residues 1-203) directly associates with the TAD (residues 526-748) with an affinity of Kd = 2 ± 1 µM.
source: We observe binding between these protein fragments and measured an affinity of Kd = 2 ± 1 µM (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The minimal FoxM1 NRD (residues 1-114) and minimal TAD (residues 696-748) associate with comparable affinity (Kd = 3 ± 2 µM).
source: Using sequence conservation we designed a minimal NRD (1-114) and minimal TAD (696-748) and found that they associate with comparable affinity (Kd = 3 ± 2 µM).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: 64% of the backbone HN, NH, Cα, and Cβ chemical shifts were assigned in the FoxM1 NRD-TAD construct.
source: We assigned 64% of the backbone HN, NH, Cα, and Cβ chemical shifts in this construct using triple-resonance backbone correlation spectra with TROSY readout.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the NMR data collection.

claim: A stretch of residues in the FoxM1 TAD adopts a β-hairpin conformation when bound to the NRD.
source: Notably, the SSI analysis suggests that a stretch of residues in the TAD adopts a β-hairpin conformation, which contrasts the helical TAD structures typically observed in complexes with co-activator domains (De Guzman et al., 2006; Goto et al., 2002; Krois et al., 2016; Radhakrishnan et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2013; Zor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift analysis and contrasted with literature on TAD structures.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD-TAD structure consists of a five-stranded pleated β-sheet and a single α-helix.
source: The NRD-TAD structure consists of a five-stranded pleated β-sheet and a single α-helix.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure determination.

claim: Three of the beta strands (β1-β3) in the FoxM1 NRD-TAD structure are from sequences in the NRD.
source: Three of the beta strands (β1-β3) are from sequences in the NRD, and two additional strands are from sequences in the TAD (β4-β5) (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Two beta strands (β4-β5) in the FoxM1 NRD-TAD structure are from sequences in the TAD.
source: Three of the beta strands (β1-β3) are from sequences in the NRD, and two additional strands are from sequences in the TAD (β4-β5) (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The amphipathic helix in the FoxM1 NRD-TAD structure is an insertion between the parallel β2 and β3 strands in the NRD.
source: The amphipathic helix is an insertion between the parallel β2 and β3 strands in the NRD.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure.

claim: One face of the helix in the FoxM1 NRD-TAD structure packs against the β-sheet to form the hydrophobic core of the structure.
source: One face of the helix packs against the β-sheet to form the hydrophobic core of the structure.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure.

claim: Sidechains from β-strands in both the FoxM1 NRD (I64, V76, I78, F106, and L108) and TAD (L709 and L716) form an extended, buried interface through highly specific interactions with helix residues (I84, I87, I88, and L91).
source: Sidechains from β−strands in both the NRD (I64, V76, I78, F106, and L108, human sequence numbering) and TAD (L709 and L716) form an extended, buried interface through highly specific, experimentally confirmed interactions with helix residues (I84, I87, I88, and L91) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by NOE data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both the FoxM1 NRD and TAD contribute essential residues to the hydrophobic core of the NRD-TAD structure.
source: The fact that both the NRD and TAD contribute essential residues to the hydrophobic core suggests the requirement of an association for forming the observed structure of both domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing interdomain contacts.

claim: Mutations on the β-sheet face of the FoxM1 NRD that is proximal to the helix inhibit binding with the TAD.
source: We find that mutations on the β-sheet face that is proximal to the helix all inhibit binding with the TAD, with mutations on the two strands closest to the TAD (V76A/I78A in β2 and F106A/L108A in β3) having the greatest effects.
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations to the hydrophobic face of the FoxM1 NRD helix (I88A and L91A) disrupt TAD binding.
source: We find that mutations to the hydrophobic face of the NRD helix (I88A and L91A) also disrupt TAD binding.
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations to the distal side of the FoxM1 NRD β-sheet result in modest or no change in TAD binding affinity.
source: In contrast, mutations to the distal side of the NRD β-sheet only result in a modest decrease in affinity (I65A or V75A) or no change in affinity (I107A/I109A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Three mutations in the FoxM1 TAD (V708A, L709A, L716A) have strong effects on NRD binding.
source: We found that three mutations have strong effects on binding (V708A, L709A, L716A), while mutation at one sidechain that points toward the distal side of the sheet (M712A) has a modest effect.
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FoxM1 mutations that destabilize the NRD-TAD interface increase FoxM1 activity in luciferase reporter assays.
source: We found that this activity is further increased upon expression of FoxM1 harboring mutations that destabilize the NRD-TAD interface.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutations closer to the FoxM1 NRD-TAD interface in NRD strands β2 and β3, the NRD helix, and the TAD have strong effects on FoxM1 activity.
source: In contrast, mutations closer to the interface in NRD strands β2 and β3, the NRD helix, and the TAD have strong effects.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WT FoxM1 activity in luciferase reporter assays is mitigated by autorepression.
source: We conclude that the WT FoxM1 activity in this assay is mitigated by autorepression and that, by destabilizing the NRD-TAD structure and association, these mutations inhibit autorepression and result in higher activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interface-disrupting mutations increase activity.

claim: Phosphorylation of the FoxM1 NRD, which contains a single conserved consensus Cdk site (S4), has minimal effect on the affinity of the NRD for the CSR-TAD.
source: We first observed that phosphorylation of the NRD, which contains a single conserved consensus Cdk site (S4), has minimal effect on the affinity of the NRD for the CSR-TAD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cdk phosphorylation of the FoxM1 CSR does not affect the NRD-TAD association.
source: The CSR-TAD construct (amino acids 526–748) binds the NRD with similar affinity whether or not it is first phosphorylated with Cdk2-CycA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cdk consensus sites has no direct effect on the repressive FoxM1 NRD-TAD interaction.
source: These measurements are consistent with the lack of Cdk sites near the NRD-TAD interface in our structural model. The observation here that phosphorylation of Cdk consensus sites has no direct effect on the repressive NRD-TAD interaction suggests that Cdk phosphorylation is not sufficient for activation of the FoxM1 transcription factor.
evidence: This is inferred from ITC binding data and the structural model.

claim: Cdk phosphorylation is not sufficient for activation of the FoxM1 transcription factor.
source: The observation here that phosphorylation of Cdk consensus sites has no direct effect on the repressive NRD-TAD interaction suggests that Cdk phosphorylation is not sufficient for activation of the FoxM1 transcription factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Cdk phosphorylation on NRD-TAD binding.

claim: The FoxM1 TAD contains five potential serine Plk1 phosphorylation sites.
source: The FoxM1 TAD contains five potential serine Plk1 phosphorylation sites.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: Plk1 quantitatively phosphorylates 4 sites (Ser702, Ser715, Ser724, and Ser741) in the FoxM1 TAD.
source: We phosphorylated the FoxM1 TAD by incubating with purified Plk1, and we confirmed quantitative phosphorylation of 4 sites (Ser702, Ser715, Ser724, and Ser741) with electrospray mass spectrometry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plk1 phosphorylation sites Ser702, Ser715, Ser724, and Ser741 in the FoxM1 TAD are all conserved.
source: These sites are all conserved (Figure 2A), and two of them (Ser715 and Ser724) were previously identified as Plk1 sites in cells (Fu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A and citation to previous literature.

claim: Ser715 and Ser724 in the FoxM1 TAD were previously identified as Plk1 sites in cells.
source: These sites are all conserved (Figure 2A), and two of them (Ser715 and Ser724) were previously identified as Plk1 sites in cells (Fu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Plk1 phosphorylated FoxM1 TAD no longer binds the NRD.
source: We observed that the Plk1 phosphorylated-TAD no longer binds the NRD by ITC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ser715 is the only Plk1 site in the FoxM1 TAD that appears near the structured NRD-TAD interface.
source: Of the four Plk1 sites, Ser715 is the only site that appears near the structured NRD-TAD interface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ser715 phosphorylation by Plk1 is necessary and sufficient for inhibiting the FoxM1 NRD-TAD association.
source: We conclude that Ser715 phosphorylation by Plk1 is necessary and sufficient for inhibiting the NRD-TAD association.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data with mutant TAD constructs.

claim: An Ser715A/Ser724A mutation decreases FoxM1 activation of several mitotic genes in U2OS cells.
source: These results are consistent with and explain the previous report that an Ser715A/Ser724A mutation decreases FoxM1 activation of several mitotic genes in U2OS cells (Fu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of Plk1 along with WT FoxM1 increases the 6DB-reporter expression 2.5-fold.
source: Similar to as previously described (Fu et al., 2008), we find that expression of Plk1 along with WT FoxM1 increases the 6DB-reporter expression 2.5-fold.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant increase in reporter expression is observed if Plk1 is expressed with a FoxM1 S715A mutant.
source: No significant increase in reporter expression is observed if Plk1 is expressed with a FoxM1 S715A mutant, which is consistent with our in vitro data demonstrating that S715 phosphorylation is necessary for TAD-NRD inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Plk1 phosphorylation of Ser715 activates FoxM1 by dissociating the repressive NRD-TAD interface.
source: These results support our model that Plk1 phosphorylation of Ser715 activates FoxM1 by dissociating the repressive NRD-TAD interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ITC and cellular assay data.

claim: Cdk phosphorylation of the FoxM1 CSR induces Plk1 association.
source: We also found using purified proteins that Cdk phosphorylation of the CSR induces Plk1 association (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming that the Plk1-FoxM1 association is direct and phosphorylation dependent.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Plk1-FoxM1 association is direct and phosphorylation dependent.
source: We also found using purified proteins that Cdk phosphorylation of the CSR induces Plk1 association (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming that the Plk1-FoxM1 association is direct and phosphorylation dependent.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: Cdk phosphorylation primes the polobox binding sites in FoxM1 and enhances Plk1 binding and phosphorylation of the TAD.
source: These results suggest that Cdk phosphorylation primes the polobox binding sites and enhances Plk1 binding and phosphorylation of the TAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Cdk phosphorylation creates Plk1 binding sites.

claim: The spectrum of the FoxM1 NRD-TAD fusion reflects the presence of structure.
source: Consistent with the NMR model, the spectrum of the fusion reflects the presence of structure.
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The FoxM1 TAD and NRD spectra indicate relatively greater disorder compared to the fusion, although they do reflect some secondary structure content.
source: In contrast, the TAD and NRD spectra indicate relatively greater disorder, although they do reflect some secondary structure content.
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The CD spectrum of the V76A/I78A FoxM1 fusion protein reflects significant disorder.
source: The CD spectrum of the V76A/I78A fusion protein also reflects significant disorder (Figure 5B), which supports the conclusion that NRD-TAD binding and structure formation are interdependent.
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FoxM1 NRD-TAD binding and structure formation are interdependent.
source: The CD spectrum of the V76A/I78A fusion protein also reflects significant disorder (Figure 5B), which supports the conclusion that NRD-TAD binding and structure formation are interdependent.
evidence: This is inferred from CD data showing that disrupting binding leads to disorder.

claim: Introduction of the V76/I78A mutation in the FoxM1 NRD alone has modest effects on the CD spectrum.
source: Notably, introduction of the same destabilizing V76/I78A mutation in the NRD alone has modest effects on the CD spectrum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the conclusion that the WT NRD alone is already considerably disordered.
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The WT FoxM1 NRD alone is already considerably disordered.
source: Notably, introduction of the same destabilizing V76/I78A mutation in the NRD alone has modest effects on the CD spectrum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the conclusion that the WT NRD alone is already considerably disordered.
evidence: This is inferred from CD data.

claim: 47 out of 50 of the non-Pro residues in the FoxM1 TAD and phosphorylated TAD were assigned by NMR.
source: 47 out of 50 of the non-Pro residues in the TAD and phosphorylated TAD were assigned.
evidence: This is a direct statement about NMR data collection.

claim: Both the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated isolated FoxM1 TAD are primarily unstructured.
source: The data support the conclusion that both the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated isolated TAD are primarily unstructured.
evidence: This is supported by NMR RCI-S2 order parameter analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The β-hairpin structure of the FoxM1 TAD is adopted upon binding to the NRD.
source: These results in comparison with the NMR data for the NRD-TAD complex (Figure 2B–2D) suggest that the β-hairpin structure of the TAD is adopted upon binding to the NRD.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing NMR data of the TAD alone versus in complex with NRD.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD is poorly structured when not in complex with the TAD.
source: In further support of the conclusion that the NRD is poorly structured when not in complex with the TAD, we found that the NRD alone elutes through a size exclusion column as expected for a protein lacking a globular structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The repressive FoxM1 NRD-TAD association drives the domains to fold into the inhibitory conformation.
source: The observations that the NRD and TAD appear unstructured when alone suggest that the repressive NRD-TAD association drives the domains to fold into the inhibitory conformation, and conversely that activation of FoxM1 is marked by an order-to-disorder structural transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the domains are disordered alone but structured when bound.

claim: Activation of FoxM1 is marked by an order-to-disorder structural transition.
source: The observations that the NRD and TAD appear unstructured when alone suggest that the repressive NRD-TAD association drives the domains to fold into the inhibitory conformation, and conversely that activation of FoxM1 is marked by an order-to-disorder structural transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation disrupts the structured complex and leads to disorder.

claim: Purified CBP TAZ2 and KIX domains bind the FoxM1 TAD.
source: We tested three common TAD interaction domains in CBP and found that purified TAZ2 and KIX domains bind the FoxM1 TAD, while TAZ1 does not (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CBP TAZ1 does not bind the FoxM1 TAD.
source: We tested three common TAD interaction domains in CBP and found that purified TAZ2 and KIX domains bind the FoxM1 TAD, while TAZ1 does not (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD-TAD fusion protein does not detectably bind to the CBP TAZ2 domain by ITC.
source: We could not detect binding of the NRD-TAD fusion protein to the TAZ2 domain using ITC, and we observed weak association to an NRD-TAD complex using NMR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data and NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FoxM1 fusion protein containing the I88A interface mutation binds CBP TAZ2 with slightly weaker affinity than the TAD alone.
source: The fusion protein containing the I88A interface mutation did bind in the ITC assay, albeit with slightly weaker affinity than the TAD alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The FoxM1 NRD inhibits FoxM1 activity by sequestering the TAD from interacting with transcriptional co-activators.
source: These results support the model that the NRD inhibits FoxM1 activity by sequestering the TAD from interacting with transcriptional co-activators.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the NRD-TAD complex does not bind CBP but the dissociated TAD does.

claim: Phosphorylation of the FoxM1 CSR-TAD by either Cdk or Plk1 does not affect the affinity with CBP TAZ2.
source: Phosphorylation of the CSR-TAD by either Cdk or Plk1 does not affect the affinity with TAZ2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TAD phosphorylation does not modulate its affinity for CBP by changing direct binding interactions.
source: We conclude that TAD phosphorylation does not modulate its affinity for CBP by changing direct binding interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from ITC data showing no change in affinity upon phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation shifts the FoxM1 NRD-TAD binding equilibrium toward TAD release from the NRD so that the TAD is accessible.
source: Instead our results indicate that phosphorylation shifts the NRD-TAD binding equilibrium toward TAD release from the NRD so that the TAD is accessible.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing phosphorylation disrupts NRD-TAD binding but doesn't affect TAD-CBP binding.

claim: TAD sequences that bind CBP typically entail contacts from hydrophobic residues along the face of one or more short amphipathic helices.
source: Binding typically entails contacts from hydrophobic residues along the face of one or more short amphipathic helices in the TAD.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about TAD-CBP interactions.

claim: Motifs such as ΦXXΦΦ or ΦΦXXΦ (Φ is a bulky hydrophobic residue and X is any residue) are commonly observed in TAD interacting sequences.
source: Motifs such as ΦXXΦΦ or ΦΦXXΦ (Φ is a bulky hydrophobic residue and X is any residue) are commonly observed in the TAD interacting sequences.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about TAD sequences.

claim: Two sequences in the FoxM1 TAD contain a ΦXXΦΦ or ΦΦXXΦ motif and appear amenable to forming amphipathic helices.
source: Two sequences in the FoxM1 TAD contain such a motif and appear amenable to forming amphipathic helices (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both sequences around residues 713-726 and 737-746 in the FoxM1 TAD are required for CBP TAZ2 binding.
source: We find that both of these sequences are required for TAZ2 binding (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data with truncated TAD constructs shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A L716A mutation in the FoxM1 TAD results in no detectable binding to CBP TAZ2.
source: We tested a L716A TAD mutant and found no detectable binding to TAZ2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The importance of L716 for CBP association explains how FoxM1 NRD binding inhibits CBP association.
source: The importance of L716 for CBP association explains how NRD binding inhibits CBP association and likely explains why the L716A mutation did not result in similar increased FoxM1 activity in the luciferase assay as other mutations in the TAD (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that L716 is important for both NRD and CBP binding.

claim: The L716A mutation disrupts both FoxM1 NRD inhibition and activation through CBP recruitment.
source: The mutation disrupts both NRD inhibition and activation through CBP recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that L716A affects both NRD and CBP binding.

claim: In the autoinhibited FoxM1 conformation, the NRD binds the TAD via a structured interface and stabilizes a β-hairpin conformation that is incompatible with co-activator binding.
source: In its autoinhibited conformation, the NRD binds the TAD via a structured interface and stabilizes a β-hairpin conformation that is incompatible with co-activator binding.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure and binding data.

claim: Cdk phosphorylation of the FoxM1 CSR domain induces Plk1 docking to FoxM1 and subsequent phosphorylation of Ser715.
source: Cdk phosphorylation of the CSR domain induces Plk1 docking to FoxM1 and subsequent phosphorylation of Ser715.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing Cdk phosphorylation creates Plk1 binding sites and mass spectrometry showing Plk1 phosphorylates Ser715.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser715 destabilizes the FoxM1 TAD β-hairpin, which releases from the NRD.
source: Phosphorylation destabilizes the TAD β-hairpin, which releases from the NRD, and both the NRD and TAD become disordered.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing phosphorylation disrupts binding and CD/NMR data showing disorder.

claim: Upon release from the NRD, both the FoxM1 NRD and TAD become disordered.
source: Phosphorylation destabilizes the TAD β-hairpin, which releases from the NRD, and both the NRD and TAD become disordered.
evidence: This is supported by CD and NMR data.

claim: The released FoxM1 TAD is free to adopt the helical conformation that is likely necessary for recruiting co-activator CBP through association with either the KIX or TAZ2 domain.
source: The TAD is free to adopt the helical conformation that is likely necessary for recruiting co-activator CBP through association with either the KIX or TAZ2 domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TADs typically bind CBP in helical conformations and the FoxM1 TAD binds KIX and TAZ2.

claim: Eukaryotic transcription factors almost invariably contain large regions of intrinsic structural disorder.
source: Eukaryotic transcription factors almost invariably contain large regions of intrinsic structural disorder, which facilitate protein-protein interactions for gene activation, posttranslational modifications for regulation, and control over nuclear localization (Minezaki et al., 2006; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intrinsic structural disorder in transcription factors facilitates protein-protein interactions for gene activation, posttranslational modifications for regulation, and control over nuclear localization.
source: Eukaryotic transcription factors almost invariably contain large regions of intrinsic structural disorder, which facilitate protein-protein interactions for gene activation, posttranslational modifications for regulation, and control over nuclear localization (Minezaki et al., 2006; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The induction of structure in transcription factors could be used to negatively regulate transcription factor activity by restricting accessibility, particularly of the transactivation domain.
source: Whereas structural disorder is required for function, it follows that the induction of structure could be used to negatively regulate transcription factor activity by restricting accessibility, particularly of the transactivation domain.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle that disorder is functional.

claim: The repressed FoxM1 TAD has a β-hairpin structure.
source: Interestingly, the repressed TAD has a β-hairpin structure, while the CBP bound state likely contains α-helical structures and involves a TAD sequence near the Ser715 phosphorylation site that overlaps with the NRD-binding sequence.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure.

claim: The CBP bound state of the FoxM1 TAD likely contains α-helical structures.
source: Interestingly, the repressed TAD has a β-hairpin structure, while the CBP bound state likely contains α-helical structures and involves a TAD sequence near the Ser715 phosphorylation site that overlaps with the NRD-binding sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the general knowledge that TADs bind CBP in helical conformations.

claim: FoxM1 regulation entails secondary structure switching of the TAD between strand, coil, and helical structures.
source: Thus, FoxM1 regulation entails secondary structure switching of the TAD between strand, coil, and helical structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different TAD structures in different states.

claim: Ser715 phosphorylation destabilizes the FoxM1 NRD-TAD association.
source: We find that Ser715 phosphorylation destabilizes the NRD-TAD association and that the dissociated TAD is intrinsically disordered and capable of binding CBP.
evidence: This is supported by ITC and NMR data.

claim: The dissociated FoxM1 TAD is intrinsically disordered and capable of binding CBP.
source: We find that Ser715 phosphorylation destabilizes the NRD-TAD association and that the dissociated TAD is intrinsically disordered and capable of binding CBP.
evidence: This is supported by NMR and ITC data.

claim: Phosphorylation has been observed to control structural transitions as a means to regulate other intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: Phosphorylation has been observed to control structural transitions as a means to regulate other intrinsically disordered proteins.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge.

claim: The transcription factor Ets-1 undergoes a disorder-to-order transition upon phosphorylation.
source: For example, both the transcription factor Ets-1 and the translation regulator 4E-BP2 undergo disorder-to-order transitions upon phosphorylation, while the nucleophosmin protein dissociates from a structured pentamer to a disordered monomer upon phosphorylation (Bah et al., 2015; Mitrea et al., 2014; Pufall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The translation regulator 4E-BP2 undergoes a disorder-to-order transition upon phosphorylation.
source: For example, both the transcription factor Ets-1 and the translation regulator 4E-BP2 undergo disorder-to-order transitions upon phosphorylation, while the nucleophosmin protein dissociates from a structured pentamer to a disordered monomer upon phosphorylation (Bah et al., 2015; Mitrea et al., 2014; Pufall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The nucleophosmin protein dissociates from a structured pentamer to a disordered monomer upon phosphorylation.
source: For example, both the transcription factor Ets-1 and the translation regulator 4E-BP2 undergo disorder-to-order transitions upon phosphorylation, while the nucleophosmin protein dissociates from a structured pentamer to a disordered monomer upon phosphorylation (Bah et al., 2015; Mitrea et al., 2014; Pufall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FoxM1 demonstrates a new example in which the order-to-disorder transition occurs coincident with modulation of an intramolecular association between domains.
source: FoxM1 demonstrates a new example in which the order-to-disorder transition occurs coincident with modulation of an intramolecular association between domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation disrupts the structured NRD-TAD complex leading to disorder.

claim: The plasticity of disordered domains and the ability to regulate the plasticity through posttranslational modifications explains why intrinsically disordered proteins are so well suited to regulate biological function.
source: This plasticity of disordered domains and the ability to regulate the plasticity through posttranslational modifications explains why intrinsically disordered proteins are so well suited to regulate biological function.
evidence: This is a general inference from the observations about FoxM1 and other disordered proteins.

claim: In the active FoxM1 conformation, in which phosphorylation inhibits the repressive NRD-TAD association, the NRD is largely disordered as well as the TAD.
source: Unexpectedly, our data indicate that in the active FoxM1 conformation, in which phosphorylation inhibits the repressive NRD-TAD association, the NRD is largely disordered as well as the TAD.
evidence: This is supported by CD and NMR data.

claim: Additional disorder in the active FoxM1 conformation may be important to increase conformational flexibility within the context of chromatin, to promote regulation of FoxM1 stability, or to contribute to the formation of low complexity domain condensates.
source: We propose that this additional disorder may be important to increase conformational flexibility within the context of chromatin, to promote regulation of FoxM1 stability, or to contribute to the formation of low complexity domain condensates as recently described (Cho et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Laoukili et al., 2008b; Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Park et al., 2008a; Wang et al., 2017; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to literature on disordered protein functions.

claim: The idea that NRDs may appear in regions of intrinsic disorder should motivate the identification of additional 'hidden' NRDs that adopt structure only upon interaction with their target.
source: While several transcription factor NRDs have been characterized (Kim et al., 1999; Park et al., 2008b; Ramsay and Gonda, 2008; Shi et al., 1995; Spengler and Brattain, 2006; Wierstra and Alves, 2006a), the idea that NRDs may appear in regions of intrinsic disorder should motivate the identification of additional 'hidden' NRDs that adopt structure only upon interaction with their target.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings about FoxM1.

claim: Multiple Cdk and Plk1 phosphorylation events have been implicated in FoxM1 activation.
source: Like many cell division regulatory proteins, FoxM1 undergoes cell-cycle dependent multisite phosphorylation. While multiple Cdk and Plk1 phosphorylation events have been implicated in FoxM1 activation, our results demonstrate that phosphorylation of one specific Plk1 site (Ser715) is directly responsible for freeing the TAD from sequestration by the NRD.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Phosphorylation of one specific Plk1 site (Ser715) is directly responsible for freeing the FoxM1 TAD from sequestration by the NRD.
source: While multiple Cdk and Plk1 phosphorylation events have been implicated in FoxM1 activation, our results demonstrate that phosphorylation of one specific Plk1 site (Ser715) is directly responsible for freeing the TAD from sequestration by the NRD.
evidence: This is supported by ITC and cellular assay data.

claim: The observation of specificity in the effects of FoxM1 phosphorylation resembles what has been proposed for the retinoblastoma protein, in which specific phosphorylation events drive distinct structural changes or protein-protein interactions.
source: Our observation of specificity in the effects of FoxM1 phosphorylation more resembles what has been proposed for the retinoblastoma protein, in which specific phosphorylation events drive distinct structural changes or protein-protein interactions (Rubin, 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to another protein supported by a citation.

claim: The identification of a structured, repressed FoxM1 conformation suggests the possibility of developing molecules that bind and stabilize the repressive NRD-TAD association or target FoxM1 for degradation.
source: The identification of a structured, repressed conformation suggests the possibility of developing molecules that bind and stabilize the repressive NRD-TAD association or target FoxM1 for degradation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the structural findings.
